title: How the Codex harness runs one coding-agent turn
subtitle: OpenAI's open-source Rust harness: context building, tool calls, sandboxing, auto review and compaction.
hook: Escalations go to a second, read-only agent that reads the transcript and judges whether you asked for it.

nodes.label: Developer
nodes.detail: A developer types a message in the Codex app or another client. Everything that follows starts when that message is sent.
nodes.tradeoff: The same open protocol also powers community clients and even a plugin that puts Codex inside Claude Code.

nodes.label: App server
nodes.detail: The app server protocol carries messages from any UI into the harness. OpenAI uses the same server to power the Codex app.
nodes.tradeoff: It is built for an open ecosystem: you can build your own agent interface on top of the Codex harness.

nodes.label: Context builder
nodes.detail: Assembles model instructions, the skills list and the tool registry. Deferred tools stay out of the window and are found later through tool search.
nodes.tradeoff: The skills list is capped at 2% of the context window; more context means more contradictions and confusion.

nodes.label: Harness loop
nodes.detail: Open-source harness written in Rust. It calls the model, runs the tools it asks for, and loops. In /goal mode it injects a continuation prompt with your objective.
nodes.tradeoff: A /goal run only ends when the model calls an update-goal tool, so concrete, checkable goals work best.

nodes.label: Responses API
nodes.detail: The harness talks to the model over the Responses API, which adds agent features like tool search, apply patch and server-side compaction.
nodes.tradeoff: At 1,000 tokens per second the network became the bottleneck, so a WebSocket mode sends only what changed.

nodes.label: Tool calls
nodes.detail: apply_patch edits files, a shell tool searches with ripgrep, a persistent Node REPL scripts the browser, and spawn_agent starts subagents.
nodes.tradeoff: The model reaches for ripgrep from training, so the harness ships ripgrep in case you lack it.

nodes.label: Sandbox
nodes.detail: All file system interactions go through a sandbox layer: Seatbelt on macOS, Bubblewrap on Linux, and a custom open-source sandbox on Windows.
nodes.tradeoff: Sandboxes bring approval fatigue, and many users switch on full access, which security teams dislike.

nodes.label: Auto review
nodes.detail: When an action needs to escape the sandbox, a separate read-only subagent gets the transcript, the tool call and a risk taxonomy, then judges user authorization and impact.
nodes.tradeoff: Context decides: deleting a .git folder is fine if you asked for it and wrong if you did not.

nodes.label: Auto compaction
nodes.detail: For runs of hours or days, compaction swaps the old context window for a new one holding a compaction item with what the agent needs.
nodes.tradeoff: It runs server side in a way the model was trained on, so performance stays the same.

flow.text: Asks Codex to delete a file the project no longer needs.
The app server protocol carries the message into the harness.
Packs instructions and skills, leaving deferred tools out of the window.
Over the Responses API, the model replies with a delete tool call.
The harness runs the call through its shell tool.
The sandbox blocks the delete, so the agent asks to escalate.
A read-only review subagent sees you asked for it and approves.
Only the tool result goes back over the WebSocket, and the loop continues.

takeaways.text: With inference at 1,000 tokens per second, the network became the bottleneck, not the model.
Write short, checkable /goal prompts: the harness loops until the model itself marks the goal achieved.
Tool search, apply patch, WebSockets and server-side compaction live in the Responses API, usable from any harness.
